```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
```

Most code that wants a cache has the same shape: a function that is slow, called again
with arguments it has seen before, by more than one session. This article walks through
that case, from a function that calls a web service to the files it downloads.

```{r}
library(dazcache)
dir <- file.path(tempdir(), "slow-work")
s <- cache(dir)
```

## A slow function

Here is a stand-in for a call to a web service: it takes a moment, and its answer
depends only on its arguments. `calls` counts how often it really runs.

```{r}
calls <- 0
fetch_rates <- function(base, date) {
  calls <<- calls + 1
  Sys.sleep(0.5)
  set.seed(as.integer(date))
  data.frame(
    currency = c("EUR", "USD", "JPY"),
    rate = round(runif(3, 0.5, 150), 4)
  )
}
```

`cache_memoise()` wraps it. Rates for a past date do not change, but give them a day's
expiry anyway, and a tag to drop them all by:

```{r}
rates <- cache_memoise(
  fetch_rates,
  s,
  expire = as.difftime(1, units = "days"),
  tags = "rates"
)

system.time(rates("CHF", as.Date("2026-10-30")))
system.time(rates("CHF", as.Date("2026-10-30")))
calls
```

The second call is read from the cache. Each call is one entry, under a key made from
the function's name and its arguments:

```{r}
rates("CHF", as.Date("2026-10-29"))
cache_keys(s, prefix = "fetch_rates/")
```

## Results outlive the session

The entries are on disk, not in this session. Close the cache, open it again, and
memoise the function again under the same name, as a new session or a scheduled job
would: the answers are already there.

```{r}
cache_close(s)
s <- cache(dir)
rates <- cache_memoise(fetch_rates, s, name = "fetch_rates")

rates("CHF", as.Date("2026-10-30"))
calls
```

Every process on the machine that opens `dir` shares them the same way: a Shiny app
and a nightly job that fills it, or parallel workers that each compute part of the
work and read what the others computed.

## When the answers change

There are three ways to throw results away, from narrow to wide.

```{r}
# One call.
cache_forget(rates, "CHF", as.Date("2026-10-30"))

# Everything tagged when it was stored.
cache_evict(s, tag = "rates")
cache_keys(s, prefix = "fetch_rates/")
```

When the function itself changes meaning, a new `version` gives it new keys. The old
entries are no longer read, and leave as they expire or as the size limit evicts them.

```{r}
rates <- cache_memoise(fetch_rates, s, name = "fetch_rates", version = 2)
cache_memoise_key(rates, "CHF", as.Date("2026-10-30"))
```

## Files you download

Some slow work produces a file: a download, an export from another tool. `codec_file()`
stores the file itself, and reading the entry gives a path to a read-only copy that
every process shares.

```{r}
download <- function(url) {
  # A stand-in for utils::download.file(url, path).
  path <- tempfile(fileext = ".csv")
  utils::write.csv(mtcars, path, row.names = FALSE)
  path
}

cached_download <- function(s, url) {
  path <- cache_get(s, url, default = NULL)
  if (is.null(path)) {
    tmp <- download(url)
    cache_set(s, url, tmp, codec = codec_file(), expire = 7 * 24 * 3600)
    unlink(tmp)
    path <- cache_get(s, url)
  }
  path
}

path <- cached_download(s, "https://example.org/mtcars.csv")
basename(path)
nrow(utils::read.csv(path))
```

The file keeps its extension, so tools that go by it read it as they would the
original.

## Code written for cachem

Packages that take a cachem cache, such as memoise and Shiny's `bindCache()`, can store
in a cache through `as_cachem()`:

```{r, eval = requireNamespace("memoise", quietly = TRUE)}
cache <- as_cachem(s)
slow_square <- function(x) {
  Sys.sleep(0.5)
  x^2
}
fast_square <- memoise::memoise(slow_square, cache = cache)

system.time(fast_square(12))
system.time(fast_square(12))
```

```{r}
cache_close(s)
unlink(dir, recursive = TRUE)
```
